blocks.text: The coffee had gone bitter on the counter when Paige told me her parents were moving into my house. She was standing at my kitchen island with one hand on a stack of mail, like she was explaining a grocery list.
“I’ve been looking at the bedrooms,” she said. “They’ll take the two upstairs.”
My son, Owen, was ten feet away. He looked down at his shoes.
Paige gave me a small smile. “Don’t make this hard on the kids.”
That was the first time she said it. It wasn’t the last.

I’m 68. I live in a lake community in northern Michigan, in the house my husband and I bought when Owen was still in grade school. The house is worth a little over a million now, which sounds like more than it is when you’ve spent 31 years replacing windows, fixing the dock, and paying taxes on waterfront property. I’m not saying I’m poor. I’m saying a number on a real estate site doesn’t mean I have a spare house tucked away.

Paige’s parents, Ron and Carol, had been having money trouble. I knew that much. I didn’t know the details, and I didn’t ask. I should have. Owen told me they might need help “for a little while,” and I assumed he meant rides to appointments or help with bills.
Instead, Paige had come to my house, walked around, and chosen bedrooms for them.
The part that hurt was Owen. He knew me. He knew I’d never agreed. He could have said so. He could have at least looked at me.
I didn’t tell him what I’d already signed. Not then.
The sale papers were in a blue folder in my desk drawer. I’d accepted an offer two days earlier, but I hadn’t told my family yet. It still felt like something I could take back if I changed my mind.

Three weeks before that kitchen conversation, I’d started sorting through the upstairs closets. My husband, Ed, had been gone for four years, and I’d kept the house mostly because I knew how to keep it. Owen and Paige brought the kids over for Sunday dinner. I knew which dock board squeaked.
I knew the furnace made a clank when the temperature dropped below 20.
But I was tired of climbing stairs with laundry baskets. I was tired of checking the sump pump every spring. And the lake, lovely as it is, doesn’t shovel its own driveway.
I’d looked at a two-bedroom condo near town. Nothing fancy. It had a small balcony and a grocery store close enough that I wouldn’t need Owen to drive me if my car was in the shop.
When I told the realtor, Diane, I was thinking about selling, she asked if I was sure.
“No,” I told her. “But I’m doing it anyway.”

I didn’t tell Owen because I knew he’d take it personally. He and Paige had talked more than once about the kids growing up near the water. Owen used to say the house would be theirs someday. I’d never promised that. Still, I didn’t correct him every time he said it.

I liked hearing that he thought of the house as home. I liked imagining the kids would keep coming over, even after I wasn’t the one putting dinner on the table. There was some selfishness in that. I wanted my family close, and I let Owen’s assumptions sit there because correcting him might have meant hearing what he really thought.

The offer on the house came from a couple moving up from Grand Rapids. They had two children, and the mother wanted to be near her sister. Their offer was $1,063,500. I remember the last three digits because I checked them about six times.
I signed the purchase agreement at Diane’s office. The sale still depended on the inspection and a few other things. Closing was set for May 30.
I was supposed to tell Owen that Sunday. Then Paige got there first.

She and Owen came over after lunch. The kids were in the car with a tablet, and Paige had a notepad in her purse. I thought she was going to ask about Mother’s Day plans. She started with Ron and Carol.
“They can’t keep renting,” she said. “The landlord’s selling.”
“They’re going to need somewhere to land.”
Owen picked at a loose thread on his shirt. I waited for him to say what he meant.
I answered before I could make myself sound nicer. “It’s my house.”
“I know,” she said. “We’ve talked it over.”
We. That was the word that made me look at Owen.

Paige pulled out her notepad and started talking about the upstairs bedrooms. Ron had a bad knee, she said, so he should have the room nearest the bathroom. Carol could use the room facing the lake. They’d bring their own bed. They might need to take down the built-in shelves.
I said, “Nobody’s taking anything down.”
He rubbed his thumb along the seam of his jeans. “Until they find a place.”
Paige looked over at me. “That could take a while.”
I said no again. I didn’t raise my voice. I didn’t need to.
Paige’s smile thinned. “You know the kids will notice.”
“That you wouldn’t help their grandparents.”
She said it softly. Like she was doing me a favor by keeping it calm.
I looked at Owen. “Is this what you want?”
He took a breath and let it out through his nose. “I don’t want to get in the middle.”
That sentence made me angrier than Paige’s whole speech.
“You’re already in the middle,” I said. “You’re my son.”
He finally looked up, but only for a second. “Please don’t turn this into a fight.”
I said, “I’m not the one moving people into my house.”
Paige put the notepad back in her purse. “We’ll talk when everyone’s less upset.”

They left without asking if I wanted to see the kids. The car stayed in the drive for maybe a minute while they buckled them in. I could hear one of the kids singing from the back seat. I stood at the window and watched the car turn toward the road.
I was mad at Paige. I was mad at Owen. Mostly, I was mad that I’d let the quiet part go on so long that they thought they could make this decision without me.
The next morning I called Diane and told her what had happened.
I looked at the blue folder on my desk. “Yes.”
I didn’t want to tell them over the phone. I wanted to do it in person, which is a nice way of saying I wanted to delay it until I felt brave.
I called Owen that evening and asked him to come by alone. He said he’d try. He didn’t come.

Paige texted me the next day. She said the kids had asked when they were going to see Grandma. She added a little heart at the end. I read the message twice, then typed, “Anytime you and Owen want to bring them.” I deleted it. I typed, “I miss them.” I deleted that too.
What I sent was, “I’m free Sunday afternoon.”
Three days later, Ron and Carol arrived with suitcases.

It was a Thursday, just before 11 in the morning. I was at the kitchen sink rinsing a mug when I heard a car door shut. Then another. I looked through the front window and saw Ron carrying a hard-sided suitcase up my steps.
Paige was right behind him with a tote bag. Owen was unloading another suitcase from the trunk. Carol stood by the car holding a folded sweater and looking toward the house.
I dried my hands on the dish towel and went to the door. I didn’t open it wide.
Paige said, “We’re going to get them settled, and then we can talk.”
Owen stopped on the walkway. Ron put his suitcase down.
